name: Old Tupi (Tupinambá)
notes: Old Tupi (Tupinambá), the língua geral of colonial Brazil, written in the normalised orthography of modern editions. Six oral vowels /a ɛ i ɔ u ɨ/ and their nasal counterparts; stops /p t k ʔ/, fricatives /β s ʃ h/, nasals /m n ŋ ɲ/, tap /ɾ/, the velar fricative /ɣ/ and the semivowels /j w ɨ̯/. ⟨b⟩ is the bilabial fricative [β], ⟨x⟩ is [ʃ], ⟨g⟩ is the velar fricative [ɣ], ⟨h⟩ is [h], ⟨ng⟩ is [ŋ], ⟨nh⟩ is [ɲ], ⟨gû⟩ is [ɡw] and ⟨'⟩ is the glottal stop. ⟨mb⟩ and ⟨nd⟩ are /m/ and /n/ before an oral vowel, realised as the prenasalised stops [ᵐb ⁿd]. Bare ⟨d⟩ is not a letter of this orthography — ⁿd is only ever spelled ⟨nd⟩ — but bare ⟨g⟩ and ⟨h⟩ are, distinct from the digraphs ⟨gû⟩ and ⟨ng⟩. The language is also the indigenous substrate node that Brazilian Portuguese resolves to for toponyms and loans (abacaxi, mandioca, capim, jacaré).

allophone_rules.notes: Regressive nasal harmony: a vowel nasalises before a following nasal consonant. /m n/ surface as the prenasalised stops [ᵐb ⁿd] before an oral vowel, and the vowel to their left is nasal in 17 of the 18 gold tokens that write the prenasalisation; before plain [m n ŋ ɲ] the gold splits 54 nasal to 57 oral, so the rule follows the standard leftward-spreading Tupí-Guaraní analysis rather than the gold's mixed practice. The rank-2 close-mid readings [e] and [o] are deliberately left out of this harmony and are never nasalised, even before the same nasal contexts: adding /e/→[ẽ] and /o/→[õ] rules leaves the 1-best transcription unchanged (PER 0.0944, WER 0.2957) but widens oracle@5 from 0.0473 to 0.0520 by adding candidates that are never the gold choice, so the rank-2 vowels are held oral to keep the n-best list tight.

orthography_standard.name: Navarro normalised orthography
orthography_standard.notes: The spelling used by modern editions and dictionaries of Old Tupi, refining Lemos Barbosa's system: ⟨y⟩ for /ɨ/, ⟨î û ŷ⟩ for the semivowels, ⟨'⟩ for the glottal stop, tilde for nasal vowels and an acute accent for stress. The colonial Jesuit spelling of the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century grammars (Anchieta's Arte de grammatica of 1595 and Figueira's) is a different orthography and is not modelled here; it writes ⟨ç⟩ and ⟨ss⟩ and has no glottal-stop letter, and the benchmark headwords carry no ⟨ç⟩ or ⟨ss⟩ at all.

stress.notes: Stress falls on the final syllable of the root by default; the acute accent marks a lexically stressed vowel elsewhere and has no segmental value. ⟨î û ŷ⟩ are semivowels and never carry stress.
